newsitem.title: USA: Congress approves historic balanced budget accord.
newsitem.headline: Congress approves historic balanced budget accord.

text.p: Congress on Thursday put the final stamp of approval on an agreement to balance the U.S. budget by 2002 and give many Americans a share in a net $85 billion tax cut in the next five years.

The budget accord, worked out during months of closed door negotiations with the Clinton administration, passed the House of Representatives 327-97 and passed the Senate 76-22. The largely bipartisan votes came as no surprise as the preliminary version had passed both chambers easily in May.
This final version reconciles minor differences between the House and Senate versions.
Even before the final vote, House committees were moving forward on its proposed cuts in spending and taxes.
If it works as advertised by both Republicans and Democrats, in five years the budget would be balanced for the first time since 1969.

Over the same time period, it calls for a net tax cut of $85 billion. To ease concerns that the tax cuts could balloon after 2002, the chairmen of the House and Senate tax-writing committees pledged to keep the spirit of the accord with a net tax cut of no more than $250 billion through 2007.

The budget does not go to President Bill Clinton for his signature, but serves as a blueprint for spending and tax legislation which will be crafted this summer and will need his approval to become law.

House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, the Ohio Republican who was a central player in months of negotiations with the White House, urged his colleagues to adhere to the budget despite pressures to revise it in the coming months.
"We have to do our best to keep that agreement even when it is uncomfortable," Kasich said on the House floor.
Budget Committee Member Democrat Ken Bentsen of Texas echoed Kasich's remarks: "We must resist any attempts to undermine it provisions."

The budget aimed to bring the deficit to zero by the year 2002 by slowing the growth of federal spending. The job of balancing the budget was made easier this year because the flow of government red ink has slowed dramatically due to economic growth and spending cuts. The deficit approached $300 billion a year in the early 1990s but is expected to be under $70 billion this year.

On Wednesday a key panel took the first concrete action to translate the budget into law. The House Ways and Means health subcommittee unanimously approved a broad plan to restructure the Medicare health care programme for the elderly and cut spending by $115 billion over five years.

The bulk of the spending cuts would come from reducing Medicare payments to hospitals, managed care and other health providers. The legislation provides new incentives to expand Medicare managed care to rural areas and allows doctors and hospitals to band together to form their own health networks.

More contentious debate was expected next week when the House Ways and Means Committee begins work on the tax portion of the plan. Republicans have as a central goal the reduction of the capital gains tax rate while the administration insists that $35 billion of the package go to help higher education.
The tax bills must originate in the House.

Apart from these two major tax and spending bills which congressional leaders hope will be cleared this summer, Congress must pass 13 annual appropriations bills. These cover everything from the national parks to space exploration and must be cleared by the Oct. 1 start of the new fiscal year.

In 1995 Republicans were blamed by the public for two government shutdowns when they attempted to use the annual money bills to advance their conservative policies. Efforts to pass legislation that would make a shutdown impossible this year have run into a White House roadblock.
